source.edition: Textbook for Class XII Part I, Reprint 2026-27

chapter.name: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
chapter.blurb: Since an inverse exists only for a one-one and onto function, and the trigonometric functions are neither over their natural domains, the chapter restricts each of the six trigonometric functions to an interval on which it is bijective, defining sin^(-1), cos^(-1), cosec^(-1), sec^(-1), tan^(-1) and cot^(-1) with their branches, principal value branches and graphs (as reflections in the line y = x). It then finds principal values, uses results such as sin(sin^(-1) x) = x and sin^(-1)(sin x) = x within the principal branch, and simplifies, proves and solves inverse trigonometric expressions by substitutions such as x = sin theta, x = tan theta and x = sec theta.

scope_in.item: Recall that a function has an inverse only if it is one-one and onto, that the inverse g of f : X -> Y has domain Y and range X, and that (f^(-1) o f)(x) = x and (f o f^(-1))(y) = y
Explain why the trigonometric functions have no inverse over their natural domains, and how restricting the domain to an interval on which the function is one-one and onto gives an inverse

Identify intervals that give branches of an inverse trigonometric function (e.g. [-3pi/2, -pi/2], [-pi/2, pi/2], [pi/2, 3pi/2] for sin^(-1); [-pi, 0], [0, pi], [pi, 2pi] for cos^(-1)) and pick out the principal value branch
State the domain and principal value range of sin^(-1) ([-1, 1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2]) and cos^(-1) ([-1, 1] -> [0, pi]), and use y = sin^(-1) x <=> sin y = x

State the domain and principal value range of cosec^(-1) (R - (-1, 1) -> [-pi/2, pi/2] - {0}), sec^(-1) (R - (-1, 1) -> [0, pi] - {pi/2}), tan^(-1) (R -> (-pi/2, pi/2)) and cot^(-1) (R -> (0, pi)), and explain each excluded point from where the original function is undefined

Describe the graph of an inverse trigonometric function as obtained from the original graph by interchanging the axes, i.e. as its reflection in the line y = x, with (a, b) on the original giving (b, a) on the inverse
Distinguish sin^(-1) x from (sin x)^(-1) = 1/sin x (and similarly for the other functions), and know that with no branch mentioned the principal value branch is meant

Find the principal value of each inverse trigonometric function at standard values, including negative arguments, and evaluate sums and differences of such principal values (Examples 1-2, Exercise 2.1)

Use sin(sin^(-1) x) = x for x in [-1, 1] and sin^(-1)(sin x) = x for x in [-pi/2, pi/2] (and similar results for the other functions) to evaluate expressions such as sin^(-1)(sin 3pi/5), cos^(-1)(cos 7pi/6), tan^(-1)(tan 3pi/4), by first rewriting the angle inside the principal range
Evaluate expressions that mix trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, e.g. tan^(-1)[2 cos(2 sin^(-1)(1/2))], tan(sin^(-1)(3/5) + cot^(-1)(3/2)), sin(tan^(-1) x)

Write inverse trigonometric expressions in the simplest form, prove results and solve simple equations by substituting x = sin theta, cos theta, tan theta, sec theta (or a sin theta, a tan theta) and using Class XI trigonometric identities, checking that the resulting angle lies in the principal range (Examples 3-5, Exercise 2.2, Miscellaneous Exercise)

scope_out.item: The standard list of properties quoted as ready-made formulas, e.g. sin^(-1)(-x) = -sin^(-1) x, cos^(-1)(-x) = pi - cos^(-1) x, sin^(-1) x + cos^(-1) x = pi/2, tan^(-1) x + cot^(-1) x = pi/2, sin^(-1)(1/x) = cosec^(-1) x, and the tan^(-1) x + tan^(-1) y and 2 tan^(-1) x formulas
scope_out.reason: This reprint's Section 2.3 (p. 27) states only sin(sin^(-1) x) = x and sin^(-1)(sin x) = x 'for suitable values of domain'; the summary (p. 32) lists nothing more. Older editions had these properties, so a model may wrongly assume them. Questions must be solvable from principal values or by substitution.

scope_out.item: Determining exactly for which values of x a property or simplification is valid
scope_out.reason: The book says explicitly (p. 27): 'We will not go into the details of these values of x in the domain as this discussion goes beyond the scope of this textbook.' The interval is always given in the question.

scope_out.item: Sketching or plotting graphs of inverse trigonometric functions, or reading their increasing/decreasing behaviour off a graph
scope_out.reason: Figures 2.1-2.6 are shown for observation only (pp. 20-25); no example or exercise asks for a graph. Only the reflection-in-y = x idea is in scope.

scope_out.item: Derivatives and integrals of inverse trigonometric functions
scope_out.reason: The introduction (p. 18) only mentions that they 'serve to define many integrals'; calculus with these functions belongs to later chapters.

scope_out.item: General solutions of trigonometric equations, or values of inverse functions on non-principal branches used in evaluation
scope_out.reason: All evaluations in the chapter use the principal value branch (Note 2, p. 26); equations in the Miscellaneous Exercise (p. 31) are solved for a single value within principal ranges.
Every range and answer in the chapter is in radian measure (pi/6, 2pi/3, ...).

scope_out.item: The historical note (Aryabhata, Bhaskara, Herschel's notation, Thales)
scope_out.reason: It is background reading on p. 33, not taught mathematics, and is not examined.

concepts.name: Why inverses need restricted domains: branches and notation
concepts.description: An inverse exists only for a one-one and onto function; the trigonometric functions are not one-one and onto over their natural domains, so their domains are restricted to intervals on which they are bijective. Each such interval gives a branch of the inverse function; the one used by default is the principal value branch. sin^(-1) x is not (sin x)^(-1) = 1/sin x.
concepts.idea: Restrict a trigonometric function to an interval where it is one-one and onto, and it gets an inverse; different intervals give different branches.
concepts.rule: If f : X -> Y is one-one and onto, its inverse g : Y -> X has domain Y and range X. Sine restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2] (or [pi/2, 3pi/2], ...) is one-one onto [-1, 1]; each interval gives a branch of sin^(-1). With no branch mentioned, the principal value branch is meant. (sin x)^(-1) = 1/sin x, which is different from sin^(-1) x.
concepts.example: sin^(-1) : [-1, 1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2] is the principal value branch; the range [pi/2, 3pi/2] gives another branch (pp. 18-19, 26).

questions.q: Explain, in terms of one-one and onto, why cosine restricted to [0, pi] has an inverse, but cosine restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2] does not.
questions.a: On [0, pi], cosine is one-one and takes every value in [-1, 1] exactly once, so it is a bijection onto [-1, 1] and has an inverse. On [-pi/2, pi/2], cos(-a) = cos a, e.g. cos(-pi/3) = cos(pi/3) = 1/2, so it is not one-one; also it only takes values in [0, 1], so it is not onto [-1, 1]. Hence no inverse exists there.
s: Shows cosine is one-one and onto [-1, 1] on [0, pi]
Shows cosine fails on [-pi/2, pi/2], e.g. cos(-pi/3) = cos(pi/3), or that it misses negative values

questions.a: (tan(pi/4))^(-1) = 1/tan(pi/4) = 1/1 = 1. tan^(-1)(1) is the angle in (-pi/2, pi/2) whose tangent is 1, i.e. pi/4. They differ because (tan x)^(-1) is a reciprocal, while tan^(-1) is the inverse function.
s: Finds (tan(pi/4))^(-1) = 1 as a reciprocal
Finds tan^(-1)(1) = pi/4 and states reciprocal vs inverse function

questions.q: sin x = sqrt(3)/2 at both x = pi/3 and x = 2pi/3. (a) Use this to explain why sine has no inverse on [0, pi]. (b) Which of the two angles is the principal value of sin^(-1)(sqrt(3)/2), and why? (c) Name one interval, other than [-pi/2, pi/2], on which sine is one-one and onto [-1, 1].
questions.a: (a) Two different angles in [0, pi] give the same sine, so sine is not one-one on [0, pi] and has no inverse there. (b) pi/3, because it lies in the principal range [-pi/2, pi/2] of sin^(-1), whereas 2pi/3 does not. (c) For example [pi/2, 3pi/2] (or [-3pi/2, -pi/2]).
s: Explains failure of one-one on [0, pi] using the two angles
Chooses pi/3 with the principal-range reason
Names a valid other interval such as [pi/2, 3pi/2]

questions.q: Consider these statements about branches of sin^(-1). (I) Corresponding to each interval on which sine is one-one and onto [-1, 1], we get a different branch of sin^(-1). (II) When no branch is mentioned, sin^(-1) x may take any value in [-pi, pi]. Which is or are correct?

A student restricts the tangent function to (pi/2, 3pi/2) and claims this gives a valid inverse of tangent. (a) Is tangent one-one and onto R on this interval? (b) Is this the principal value branch? (c) Compare the value of tan^(-1)(1) on this branch with its principal value.
questions.a: (a) Yes. The book lists (pi/2, 3pi/2) among the intervals on which tangent is bijective with range R, so it does give a branch of tan^(-1). (b) No; the principal value branch of tan^(-1) has range (-pi/2, pi/2). (c) On this branch tan^(-1)(1) = 5pi/4, since tan(5pi/4) = 1 and 5pi/4 lies in (pi/2, 3pi/2); the principal value is pi/4.
s: States tangent is one-one onto R on (pi/2, 3pi/2), so it is a branch
States it is not the principal branch, which is (-pi/2, pi/2)
Gives 5pi/4 on this branch and pi/4 as principal value

questions.q: Ravi says: 'Because the sine function repeats its values, sin^(-1) can never be defined as a function.' Evaluate Ravi's claim.
questions.a: Ravi is wrong. Sine is not one-one on R, but if its domain is restricted to an interval such as [-pi/2, pi/2], it becomes one-one and onto [-1, 1]. Then sin^(-1) : [-1, 1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2] is a well-defined function (the principal value branch).
s: States the claim is incorrect
Justifies by restricting the domain to [-pi/2, pi/2] so sine becomes one-one and onto [-1, 1]

questions.q: Choose an interval, different from [0, pi], on which cosine is one-one and onto [-1, 1]. For the branch of cos^(-1) that it gives, state the domain and range, and find the value this branch gives for cos^(-1)(1/2).
questions.a: Example: [pi, 2pi]. Cosine rises from -1 at pi to 1 at 2pi, taking each value once, so it is one-one and onto [-1, 1]. The branch is cos^(-1) : [-1, 1] -> [pi, 2pi]. On it, cos^(-1)(1/2) = 5pi/3, since cos(5pi/3) = 1/2 and 5pi/3 lies in [pi, 2pi]. (Using [-pi, 0] instead gives -pi/3.)
s: Chooses a valid interval such as [pi, 2pi] or [-pi, 0]
States domain [-1, 1] and the chosen interval as range
Finds the correct value in that branch, e.g. 5pi/3 or -pi/3

concepts.name: sin^(-1) and cos^(-1): domain, principal range and graph
concepts.description: sin^(-1) : [-1, 1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2] and cos^(-1) : [-1, 1] -> [0, pi]; y = sin^(-1) x means sin y = x; the graph of the inverse is obtained by interchanging the axes, i.e. as the reflection of the original graph in the line y = x.
concepts.idea: Both functions take inputs from [-1, 1]; sin^(-1) returns angles in [-pi/2, pi/2], cos^(-1) returns angles in [0, pi].
concepts.rule: y = sin^(-1) x means sin y = x with y in [-pi/2, pi/2]; y = cos^(-1) x means cos y = x with y in [0, pi]. If (a, b) is on the graph of the original function, (b, a) is on the graph of the inverse.
concepts.example: sin^(-1)(-1) = -pi/2 and cos^(-1)(-1) = pi; (pi/6, 1/2) on y = sin x gives (1/2, pi/6) on y = sin^(-1) x (pp. 19-21).

questions.q: Find a number x in [-1, 1] for which sin^(-1) x and cos^(-1) x have the same principal value. Justify by computing both.
questions.a: Take x = 1/sqrt(2). sin^(-1)(1/sqrt(2)) = pi/4 since sin(pi/4) = 1/sqrt(2) and pi/4 is in [-pi/2, pi/2]. cos^(-1)(1/sqrt(2)) = pi/4 since cos(pi/4) = 1/sqrt(2) and pi/4 is in [0, pi]. Both equal pi/4.

concepts.name: cosec^(-1), sec^(-1), tan^(-1), cot^(-1): domains and principal ranges
concepts.description: The principal value branches cosec^(-1) : R - (-1, 1) -> [-pi/2, pi/2] - {0}, sec^(-1) : R - (-1, 1) -> [0, pi] - {pi/2}, tan^(-1) : R -> (-pi/2, pi/2) and cot^(-1) : R -> (0, pi), and why each excluded point or open end is excluded.
concepts.idea: The excluded points in each range are exactly where the original function is undefined.
concepts.rule: cosec^(-1): domain R - (-1, 1), range [-pi/2, pi/2] - {0}. sec^(-1): domain R - (-1, 1), range [0, pi] - {pi/2}. tan^(-1): domain R, range (-pi/2, pi/2). cot^(-1): domain R, range (0, pi).
concepts.example: sec^(-1)(1/2) is undefined because 1/2 lies in (-1, 1); tan^(-1) x can never equal pi/2 because tan(pi/2) is not defined (pp. 21-25, 32).

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) tan^(-1) x is defined for every real number x. (II) The principal range (0, pi) of cot^(-1) contains the value pi/2. Which is or are correct?
cos^(-1)(1/2) is defined, but sec^(-1)(1/2) is not, even though sec x = 1/cos x. Explain why, and then find the principal value of sec^(-1)(2).
questions.a: cos^(-1)(1/2) is defined because 1/2 lies in [-1, 1], the domain of cos^(-1); its value is pi/3. sec^(-1)(1/2) would need an angle y with sec y = 1/2, i.e. cos y = 2, which is impossible; equivalently 1/2 is not in the domain R - (-1, 1) of sec^(-1). For sec^(-1)(2): sec y = 2 means cos y = 1/2, and the angle in [0, pi] - {pi/2} is pi/3.
s: Explains cos^(-1)(1/2) is defined since 1/2 is in [-1, 1]
Explains sec^(-1)(1/2) is undefined since 1/2 is not in R - (-1, 1) (cos y = 2 impossible)
Finds sec^(-1)(2) = pi/3

questions.q: Arjun says: 'Since the principal range of tan^(-1) is (-pi/2, pi/2), tan^(-1) x equals pi/2 when x is very large.' Evaluate Arjun's claim.
questions.a: Arjun is wrong. The interval (-pi/2, pi/2) is open, so pi/2 itself is not in the range. If tan^(-1) x = pi/2, then x = tan(pi/2), which is not defined, so no real x gives tan^(-1) x = pi/2.
s: States the claim is false
Explains pi/2 is excluded because tan(pi/2) is not defined (open interval)

questions.q: Give one real number x, other than 1 and -1, for which sec^(-1) x, cosec^(-1) x, tan^(-1) x and cot^(-1) x are all defined, and one real number for which tan^(-1) x and cot^(-1) x are defined but sec^(-1) x and cosec^(-1) x are not. Justify both.

concepts.name: Finding principal values
concepts.description: Finding the principal value of an inverse trigonometric function at a standard value, including negative arguments, by choosing the angle that lies in the principal range; evaluating sums and differences of such principal values.
concepts.idea: Of all angles with the given trigonometric value, the principal value is the one inside the principal range.
concepts.rule: Let y = f^(-1)(a), so f(y) = a; find the standard angle, then adjust (e.g. pi - angle for cos^(-1) and cot^(-1) of negative values, minus the angle for sin^(-1) and tan^(-1)) so that y lies in the principal range.
concepts.example: cot^(-1)(-1/sqrt(3)) = 2pi/3, since cot(2pi/3) = -1/sqrt(3) and 2pi/3 lies in (0, pi) (Example 2, p. 26).

concepts.name: Composing a function with its inverse
concepts.description: sin(sin^(-1) x) = x for x in [-1, 1] and sin^(-1)(sin x) = x for x in [-pi/2, pi/2], with similar results for the other functions; evaluating expressions such as sin^(-1)(sin 3pi/5) or cos^(-1)(cos 7pi/6) by first rewriting the angle inside the principal range; values of expressions mixing trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions.
concepts.idea: f(f^(-1) x) = x needs only x in the domain; f^(-1)(f(x)) = x needs x in the principal range.
concepts.rule: sin(sin^(-1) x) = x, x in [-1, 1]; sin^(-1)(sin x) = x, x in [-pi/2, pi/2]. If x is outside the principal range, replace it by an angle in the range with the same trigonometric value (e.g. sin(pi - x) = sin x).

concepts.name: Simplifying and proving by trigonometric substitution
concepts.description: Writing an inverse trigonometric expression in the simplest form, or proving an identity or solving an equation, by substituting x = sin theta, cos theta, tan theta or sec theta (or a sin theta, a tan theta), using Class XI trigonometric identities, and checking that the resulting angle lies in the principal range.
concepts.idea: A clever substitution turns the algebraic expression inside into sin, cos or tan of a single angle, so the inverse function undoes it.
concepts.rule: Put x = sin theta (etc.), simplify using identities such as sin 2theta = 2 sin theta cos theta, sec^2 theta - 1 = tan^2 theta, (1 - tan theta)/(1 + tan theta) = tan(pi/4 - theta), then use f^(-1)(f(angle)) = angle only after checking the angle lies in the principal range for the given interval of x.
concepts.example: With x = sin theta, sin^(-1)(2x sqrt(1 - x^2)) = sin^(-1)(sin 2theta) = 2 sin^(-1) x for -1/sqrt(2) <= x <= 1/sqrt(2) (Example 3, p. 28).
